new_statements.rule_in_words: The source treats Kandawo as (probably) a pitch accent language: one syllable per word is prominent ('stressed') and carries a high level pitch, the others lower falling pitch; it gives NO rule for which syllable is prominent, and notes pitch minimal pairs on monosyllables, so prominence/pitch is at least partly lexical and may be tonal rather than accentual. Orthography does not write tone (p.5).
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic minimal pairs distinguished by pitch (implying some words are 'completely unstressed'); question and surprise particles are 'expressed tonally' (p.5). Author explicitly flags the analysis as provisional.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement based on citation forms in an Organised Phonology Data sheet; no phrase-level discussion; no acoustic data. Position of the accent is left undetermined, so this is a 'pitch accent, placement unstated/lexical' record rather than a positional stress rule.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD describes 'Kandawo (Ganja, Kajawo, Narake) [gam]', Jiwaka Province, major villages Ambullua, Mogum, Mame, Gepal, Guma, Yawaremol (Upper Jimi; Graham's 'dialect 1' area) = Glottolog kand1303. Wurm (1975: n.7) treated Gandja/Kandawo and Narak [nac, nara1234?] as aberrant dialects of one language; SIL and Glottolog keep them separate. Glottolog's Berndt 1954 reference is mis-attached (its 'Kafe' is Kamano-Kafe, not Kandawo).

sources.note: p.4 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': Kandawo 'appears to be a pitch accent language', stressed syllable bears high flat pitch, unstressed syllables lower falling pitch; monosyllabic minimal (pitch) pairs exist, so either stress is not required or the tonal system is more complex; no rule for the position of the stressed syllable is given; 'much more research is needed'. p.5: 'Tone is not written'; question/surprise particles are 'expressed tonally'.
